paragraphs: This paper studies an inverse problem: recovering a function when the available information consists of its conditional averages. Conditional kernel mean embeddings provide a flexible way to represent those averages without committing to a fixed parametric model. Recovering the function behind them, however, requires a way to reverse the averaging relationship.

The authors formalize deconditional kernel mean embeddings for this purpose and interpret them as a nonparametric version of Bayes’ rule. Their central connection is to task transformed Gaussian processes. They show that deconditional kernel means correspond to the posterior predictive mean in this probabilistic framework, linking the reconstruction method to Bayesian inference.

That connection supplies more than an alternative interpretation. It provides uncertainty estimates, explains the role of regularization parameters, and exposes a marginal likelihood for learning kernel hyperparameters. The resulting framework therefore connects function recovery, uncertainty, and parameter selection within one account. The abstract identifies likelihood-free inference and sparse representations for large datasets as practical applications enabled by these developments.
icml-2019-bayesian-deconditional-kernel-.tldr: The paper gives deconditional kernel mean embeddings a Gaussian-process interpretation that supports function recovery, uncertainty estimation, and hyperparameter learning.

paragraphs: When data or losses have heavy tails, unusually large observations can make learning from a finite sample difficult. Algorithms that minimize average training loss may then need many observations to perform well on new data. This paper targets that problem by changing how the direction of improvement is estimated during learning.

The proposed technique constructs a computationally inexpensive, robust estimate of the risk gradient through an iterative procedure. That estimate can be supplied to a steepest descent method. The intervention is therefore at the level of the information used to choose an update: the method seeks a reliable gradient estimate under weaker statistical assumptions.

The authors provide finite-sample risk bounds under weak moment assumptions on the loss gradient. Simulations and experiments on real data illustrate that learning can become more efficient and reliable without knowing the loss tails beforehand. Together, the theory and experiments support robust gradient estimation as a practical route to better generalization when ordinary sample averages are difficult to estimate reliably.
icml-2019-better-generalization-with-les.tldr: Robust estimates of the risk gradient can improve learning with heavy-tailed data under weak moment assumptions, without prior knowledge of the loss tails.

paragraphs: Positive-unlabeled learning addresses classification problems where positive examples are labeled but the remaining data mix both classes. This is useful when the negative class is too diverse to label comprehensively. Yet a limited collection of labeled negatives may still be easy to obtain, even if it covers only a narrow part of that class.

The paper introduces a framework that uses this biased negative collection alongside positive and unlabeled data. Its method is based on empirical risk minimization and can be understood as example weighting. A preliminary step inspired by positive-unlabeled learning determines the weights, allowing the training procedure to incorporate negative labels without treating their collection as representative of all negatives.

The authors derive an estimation error bound and report effective results on several benchmark datasets. Their experiments cover both the proposed setting with biased negatives and ordinary positive-unlabeled learning. The contribution is a way to make use of incomplete negative supervision while explicitly accounting for its selective coverage, rather than requiring a fully representative negative training set.
icml-2019-classification-from-positive-u.tldr: An example-weighting method incorporates selectively labeled negatives into positive-unlabeled classification, with an estimation bound and supporting benchmark results.

paragraphs: Combining independently trained models becomes difficult when they use different architectures and cannot expose their local data or internal structure. Those constraints arise especially in information-sensitive settings. This paper studies how multiple such experts can pool their predictive expertise while operating as black boxes to one another.

The proposed collective model fusion framework addresses three linked problems. Experts must interact in ways that reveal their predictive behavior, turn what they learn about one another into representations that can be shared efficiently, and combine those representations into a consensus prediction. This organizes collaboration around externally accessible behavior despite differences in the experts’ internal designs.

The authors analyze the resulting framework theoretically and demonstrate it empirically on several datasets. The contribution is a framework for cooperation among heterogeneous models under restricted access, including both the exchange of information and its use in collective prediction. Its stated objective is improved predictive performance through shared expertise, with theoretical analysis and experiments supporting the proposed approach.
icml-2019-collective-model-fusion-for-mu.tldr: The paper develops and evaluates a framework for heterogeneous black-box experts to share predictive knowledge and produce consensus predictions.

paragraphs: A network with piecewise linear activations divides its input space into regions, each governed by a linear function. Counting these regions measures one aspect of its expressive capacity. Although specially constructed networks can have exponentially many regions as depth increases, that possibility does not establish how much complexity ordinary networks actually exhibit.

The paper develops a mathematical framework for counting regions and measuring the boundaries between them. At initialization, it proves that the average number of regions encountered along any one-dimensional subspace grows linearly with the total neuron count. It also finds that the average distance to the nearest boundary scales inversely with the number of neurons.

These results distinguish achievable architectural complexity from typical behavior at initialization. For trained networks, the conclusion is more qualified: the theory suggests region counts remain far below exponential, and the authors’ empirical observations agree with that suggestion. The work therefore provides a way to quantify a likely gap between maximum theoretical expressivity and the expressivity realized in practice.
icml-2019-complexity-of-linear-regions-i.tldr: Typical initialized networks have far fewer linear regions along one-dimensional subspaces than exponential expressivity bounds permit, with evidence suggesting a similar gap after training.

paragraphs: A learned representation can be useful because of how its points connect, as well as what information they retain. This paper develops a way to control connectivity in an autoencoder’s latent space. The aim is to give that space a structure that a subsequent learning procedure can explicitly use.

The authors introduce a loss built from persistent homology, which supplies information about connectivity. They show that the loss is differentiable under mild conditions and analyze the properties it induces. For an application, they consider one-class learning, where the task involves modeling an in-class distribution. The imposed structure helps guide parameter selection for kernel density estimation.

On computer vision data, the resulting one-class models achieve competitive performance and outperform other methods by a large margin when few samples are available. The results also indicate that an autoencoder trained on auxiliary unlabeled data can provide a latent mapping reusable across datasets. This suggests that deliberately shaping representation connectivity can support both downstream modeling choices and reuse of the learned representation.
icml-2019-connectivity-optimized-represe.tldr: A persistent-homology loss shapes latent-space connectivity and supports effective one-class learning, especially in the tested low-sample setting.

paragraphs: Distribution estimation often seeks a method that performs well against the hardest possible distribution. Such worst-case protection can leave accuracy available when the actual distribution is simpler. Two alternatives address this: assuming a useful structure in advance, or competing with an estimator given extra information while allowing a small excess error.

This paper combines those approaches in a single estimator. Its excess error vanishes at a universal rate as more samples arrive, and also vanishes as the unknown distribution becomes simpler. The second guarantee makes simplicity useful without requiring the learner to know the underlying structure beforehand. The method therefore adapts along both sample-size and distribution-complexity dimensions.

The authors show improved performance guarantees for numerous existing results in competitive and structural estimation. They also establish near-linear running time and robustness to model misspecification and permutations of domain symbols. These properties matter because the theoretical adaptation is accompanied by computational efficiency and does not rely on a particular naming of outcomes or an exactly correct structural model.
icml-2019-doubly-competitive-distributio.tldr: A single efficient distribution estimator improves its competitive guarantee both with more samples and with simpler unknown distributions.

paragraphs: Generative flow models support exact likelihood optimization and efficient image generation. This paper focuses on making their convolutional transformations more flexible. It extends the invertible 1-by-1 convolutions used in Glow to invertible d-by-d convolutions, enabling a transformation to operate across spatial positions as well as image channels.

The authors propose two constructions that preserve invertibility while giving the transformations receptive fields like those of standard convolutions. Emerging convolutions chain together particular autoregressive convolutions. Periodic convolutions use a frequency-domain representation in which the convolution can be decoupled. These provide different routes to introducing spatial interactions into an invertible flow component.

Experiments on galaxy images, CIFAR10, and ImageNet show significant improvements in generative-flow performance from the added flexibility. The findings support the value of expanding the spatial reach of invertible convolutions within these models. The contribution connects a concrete architectural change with observed improvements while retaining the invertible transformation structure needed by the flow framework.
icml-2019-emerging-convolutions-for-gene.tldr: Two constructions extend invertible flow convolutions across spatial positions and channels, improving performance on the tested image datasets.

paragraphs: GAN training is difficult because the interacting objectives are nonconvex, and optimization-based analyses typically provide only local convergence results. This paper changes the formulation by considering mixed Nash equilibria. In this perspective, the players can use distributions over strategies, expanding the object being learned beyond a single strategy for each player.

Using a classical lifting construction, the authors show that essentially all existing GAN objectives can be relaxed into mixed-strategy forms whose global optima can be solved through sampling. They then propose a mean-approximation sampling scheme. This makes methods for bi-affine games available as a systematic basis for practical GAN training algorithms.

The distinction between the relaxed formulation and its practical algorithms is central to interpreting the result. The global-optimum claim concerns the mixed-strategy forms; the experiments provide evidence about the proposed training approach. Those experiments show comparable or superior results to contemporary training algorithms and improvements over SGD, Adam, and RMSProp. The work thus links a game-theoretic reformulation to empirically effective training procedures.
icml-2019-finding-mixed-nash-equilibria-.tldr: Reformulating GAN objectives as mixed-strategy games motivates sampling-based training methods with competitive or improved experimental performance.

paragraphs: Flow-based generative models offer exact likelihoods together with efficient sampling and inference. Their density modeling performance, however, has generally lagged behind that of leading autoregressive models. Flow++ investigates whether choices inside the flow architecture help explain this gap and whether changing those choices can improve image density estimation.

The paper examines three restrictions in earlier designs: using uniform noise for dequantization, relying on affine flows with limited expressiveness, and using only convolutional conditioning networks inside coupling layers. Flow++ combines improvements to these choices. The approach treats the way data enter the model, the transformations themselves, and their conditioning networks as connected opportunities for better modeling.

The resulting model achieves the reported state of the art among non-autoregressive models for unconditional density estimation on standard image benchmarks. That is a claim about a particular model category and task, rather than a claim of surpassing all autoregressive models. The findings show progress toward narrowing the density modeling gap while building on the computational appeal of flows.
icml-2019-flow-improving-flow-based-gene.tldr: Flow++ improves dequantization and flow architecture to advance non-autoregressive image density estimation and narrow the gap with autoregressive models.

paragraphs: This paper asks how accurately item qualities can be recovered from noisy pairwise comparisons when only certain pairs are compared. The permitted comparisons form a fixed graph. Every neighboring pair is compared k times under the Bradley-Terry-Luce model, in which winning probabilities depend on the relative qualities of the two items.

The authors focus on the regime where k is large and identify graph resistance as the relevant feature of the comparison structure. They provide an algorithm whose relative estimation error scales with the square root of that resistance. This ties the quality of estimation to a specific property of how comparisons connect the items.

A lower bound shows that, apart from logarithmic factors, better dependence on graph resistance is impossible in the asymptotic setting studied. The algorithm’s guarantee also improves earlier results in its dependence on the graph and on the skewness of item qualities. Together, the upper and lower bounds explain which aspect of comparison structure governs achievable accuracy when many repeated comparisons are available.
icml-2019-graph-resistance-and-learning-.tldr: For many repeated Bradley-Terry-Luce comparisons, graph resistance determines achievable relative estimation accuracy up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how well one policy would perform using experience collected by another policy. Importance sampling adjusts observed returns according to how likely they are under the target and data-collecting policies. This paper asks whether those adjustments can improve when the data-collecting policy is estimated from the evaluation data itself.

The authors find that this shared-data estimate often produces lower mean squared error than using either the true behavior policy or a policy estimated from separate data. Their explanation is that the fitted policy helps correct action-space sampling error. Knowing the true policy describes the sampling mechanism, but does not directly account for the particular action frequencies realized in a finite dataset.

Experiments extend the finding to other popular importance-sampling variants. They also show that estimating a history-dependent behavior policy can further reduce large-sample mean squared error even when the true policy is Markovian. These are qualified improvements rather than universal guarantees, but they demonstrate that estimating a known component can sometimes improve the final evaluation.
icml-2019-importance-sampling-policy-eva.tldr: Estimating the behavior policy from the evaluation data often reduces importance-sampling error, even compared with using the true behavior policy.

paragraphs: Training methods that use sampled examples must decide which examples to select at each iteration. This paper studies that choice for variance-reduced optimization with nonconvex losses. It develops importance-sampling variants of SVRG, SAGA, and SARAH, bringing unequal sampling choices into methods designed to reduce noise in optimization updates.

The common foundation is an analysis that permits arbitrary randomized selection of subsets of examples. This includes mini-batches and supports improved mini-batch guarantees through importance sampling. In some regimes, the analysis yields superlinear speedup with respect to batch size: increasing the batch can deliver a more-than-proportional improvement in the relevant convergence behavior.

On real datasets, the methods have the capacity to accelerate training by an order of magnitude relative to the stated prior state of the art. The paper also supplies a new importance-sampling analysis of SARAH for convex objectives. Its main contribution is a general analytical framework that connects sampling design to optimization performance, with unusually strong gains possible in particular regimes.
icml-2019-nonconvex-variance-reduced-opt.tldr: A general sampling analysis enables importance-sampled variance-reduced methods for nonconvex learning, with substantial acceleration possible in certain settings.

paragraphs: A deep network’s activation function and initial weights affect how information travels through its layers before learning begins. Poor choices can erase input information during forward propagation or make gradients shrink or grow exponentially during back-propagation. These effects motivate studying random, untrained networks to understand conditions that support effective training.

The paper provides a theoretical analysis of the parameter regime called the Edge of Chaos. Earlier work connected this regime to whether deep feedforward networks could train successfully. Here, the authors focus on how the activation function and initialization parameters can be tuned to accelerate training and improve overall performance.

The resulting contribution is a theoretical account of how these design choices can work together, rather than treating activation selection and initialization as unrelated decisions. The authors show that tuning both can improve training speed and performance. The significance is that properties visible before optimization begins can guide choices that affect learning afterward, linking the behavior of random networks to practical training outcomes.
icml-2019-on-the-impact-of-the-activatio.tldr: A theoretical analysis of the Edge of Chaos shows how jointly tuning activations and initialization can accelerate training and improve performance.

paragraphs: A decision system can satisfy an equality criterion at the moment it allocates opportunities while still influencing how a population changes afterward. This paper studies that longer-term perspective on fairness. It asks how people’s responses to algorithmic decisions can reshape qualifications and group differences over time.

The authors propose an effort-based fairness measure and a data-driven framework for analyzing population change. A model of individual responses draws on social learning and equality of opportunity. Existing segregation measures from sociology and economics then quantify the population-level consequences. This connects a description of individual adaptation to a way of assessing changes across groups.

The findings indicate that different decision-making models may move group-conditional qualification distributions in different directions. Thus, an assessment based only on current allocations can miss consequences produced through later responses. The framework makes those modeled consequences part of the fairness discussion, while the paper’s conclusion raises questions about how fairness should be formalized when policies help change the populations they evaluate.
icml-2019-on-the-long-term-impact-of-alg.tldr: An effort-based fairness framework models how responses to algorithmic decisions can reshape group qualifications and population segregation over time.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a large pretrained language model works well for transfer learning, but serving many tasks means maintaining a separate full model for each one. This paper proposes adapter modules as a more compact approach. Each task receives a small set of trainable additions while the original network’s parameters remain fixed.

The design allows extensive parameter sharing across tasks and supports adding new tasks without revisiting previous ones. Its practical appeal comes from concentrating task-specific learning in a small part of the overall system. The shared pretrained network supplies a common foundation, while the adapters provide the parameters that change for each task.

The authors evaluate this approach by transferring BERT to 26 text classification tasks, including GLUE. Adapters achieve near state-of-the-art performance. On GLUE, they come within 0.8% of full fine-tuning performance while adding 3.6% parameters per task, compared with training all parameters for each fully fine-tuned model. These results demonstrate a favorable empirical tradeoff between task performance and the amount of task-specific parameterization.
icml-2019-parameter-efficient-transfer-l.tldr: Small task-specific adapters keep BERT’s original parameters fixed while achieving performance close to full fine-tuning with far fewer added parameters.

paragraphs: An agent solving a complex task may need to reason about consequences far into the future. Options provide temporal abstraction: they let the agent reason using extended behaviors rather than only individual steps. However, the underlying Markov decision process’s discount factor still determines the effective horizon in the usual options framework.

This paper modifies that framework so the agent’s horizon scales naturally with option length. The proposed option-step discount makes the relationship between temporal abstraction and discounting part of the method itself. Longer options can therefore be accompanied by a correspondingly scaled reasoning horizon, addressing a mismatch between the timescale of decisions and the horizon imposed by the underlying process.

The authors show that this discount controls a bias-variance tradeoff. In particular, larger discounts lead to less estimation variance, a relationship they identify as counterintuitive. The finding means the discount affects both the temporal reach of reasoning and the statistical behavior of estimates. It supplies a way to examine those effects together when choosing how an agent reasons over extended actions.
icml-2019-per-decision-option-discountin.tldr: Option-step discounting scales an agent’s horizon with option length and controls a bias-variance tradeoff in which larger discounts reduce estimation variance.

paragraphs: Data augmentation can improve generalization, but choosing which transformations to use creates a large search problem. Highly effective search methods can demand too much computation for ordinary use. This paper introduces Population Based Augmentation, or PBA, to make automated augmentation selection substantially less expensive.

PBA learns a schedule of augmentation policies that changes during training. This means the output of the search specifies how augmentation should evolve, rather than supplying one policy to apply throughout learning. The distinction makes training time part of the augmentation design and provides a different object for the search procedure to optimize.

The authors report that PBA matches AutoAugment’s performance on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN while using three orders of magnitude less overall computation. On CIFAR-10, its mean test error is 1.46%, a slight improvement over the stated state of the art. These findings show that changing augmentation schedules can support strong benchmark performance with a much more accessible computational cost for policy search.
icml-2019-population-based-augmentation-.tldr: PBA learns changing augmentation schedules that match AutoAugment on three benchmarks with roughly a thousandfold reduction in overall computation.

paragraphs: Without a reward signal, an agent still needs an objective if it is to explore purposefully. This paper studies objectives determined entirely by how often the agent visits different states. One example is making the state-visitation distribution as uniform as possible, with entropy measuring how broadly visits are spread.

The authors develop an efficient algorithm for these intrinsically defined objectives using a black-box planning oracle that is robust to function approximation. The central optimization tool is the conditional gradient, or Frank-Wolfe, method, combined with an approximate solver for the Markov decision process. This connects a desired visitation pattern to the policies needed to produce it.

For tabular environments with sample-based access, the authors prove efficiency in both sample requirements and computation. These guarantees apply to the specified setting, while the broader algorithm is framed through access to the planning oracle. The contribution establishes that reward-free exploration can be organized around explicit distributional objectives and, under the stated access conditions, optimized with provable efficiency.
icml-2019-provably-efficient-maximum-ent.tldr: A planning-based algorithm optimizes reward-free state-visitation objectives, including maximum entropy, with sample and computational guarantees in the tabular setting.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient methods can sample training components with replacement or process them without replacement through random shuffling. This paper gives finite-time results showing when the shuffled version converges faster. Such results identify an advantage after a bounded amount of training, rather than only describing behavior in an eventual asymptotic limit.

For strongly convex, second-order smooth functions, the authors prove a convergence rate of O(1/T² + n³/T³), where T counts iterations and n counts objective components. This implies an advantage over the O(1/T) rate of ordinary SGD after O(√n) epochs. The explicit dependence on n is central to the analysis and is generally unavoidable without further changes.

The paper also studies settings motivated by sparse data and over-parameterization. It obtains an O(1/T²) rate for sparse data and shows an advantage after any number of iterations in a setting closely related to over-parameterization. Extensions cover smooth convex and nonconvex functions. These results clarify how the benefit of shuffling depends on objective structure, dataset size, and training duration.
icml-2019-random-shuffling-beats-sgd-aft.tldr: Under stated smoothness and convexity assumptions, random shuffling has a provably faster convergence rate than sampling with replacement after finitely many epochs.

paragraphs: Sequential decisions can affect whether a participant remains available for future interactions. A disappointing outcome may end the relationship entirely, making continued participation part of the objective. This paper models that issue as lifetime maximization in a linear bandit problem with reneging, meaning participants can disengage after an unsatisfactory result.

The model gives each participant a distinct satisfaction threshold. An outcome below that threshold causes departure. It also allows outcome variance to depend on context, so uncertainty is not assumed to be the same across situations. Together, these features connect decisions to both the distribution of immediate outcomes and the possibility of losing future interactions.

The authors develop HR-UCB, a policy based on the upper-confidence-bound approach, and prove regret of O(√(T(log T)³)). They also validate its performance through simulations. The contribution is a decision-making framework that explicitly includes participant departure and context-dependent variability, accompanied by a policy with a theoretical performance guarantee. The reported empirical support comes from simulated interactions under this modeling approach.
icml-2019-stay-with-me-lifetime-maximiza.tldr: HR-UCB addresses lifetime maximization when participants leave after unsatisfactory outcomes and outcome variance depends on context, with a regret bound and simulation evidence.

paragraphs: Many selection problems balance a benefit against the cost of chosen items, so their total objective can be negative. This paper shows that useful approximation guarantees remain possible when the objective has a particular decomposition: g minus c, with g monotone, nonnegative, and weakly submodular, and c a nonnegative additive cost.

For a limit of k selected items, the algorithm returns a random feasible set whose expected value is at least (1 − e^(−γ) − ε) times the optimal set’s benefit, minus that set’s full cost. This separate treatment of benefit and cost matters: the guarantee is not simply a multiplicative approximation to their difference. Its running time is independent of k.

The method varies the relative emphasis on benefit and cost through a surrogate objective and searches geometrically over possible weak-submodularity parameters. An unconstrained version achieves the same guarantee with faster runtime. A value-oracle hardness result limits possible improvements by polynomial-time algorithms. Experiments on experimental design and directed vertex cover complement the theoretical results.
icml-2019-submodular-maximization-beyond.tldr: Fast algorithms obtain strong benefit-minus-cost guarantees for structured weakly submodular objectives even when the total objective can be negative.

paragraphs: Selecting a useful subset of observations can make parameter estimation more efficient. For quadratic measurement models, however, the moment matrix of the optimal estimator is generally unknown. Earlier approaches often linearize the observation model before evaluating selection criteria, which changes the relationships expressed by the original quadratic measurements.

This paper derives new optimality criteria through a connection to Van Trees’ inequality. The aim is to evaluate observation choices while preserving the model’s relational structure. The criteria offer a route to selection that is tailored to quadratic observations, rather than relying on the same kind of linear approximation to make the problem manageable.

Under certain conditions on the problem parameters, the authors prove that these criteria are monotone and submodular or weakly submodular. Those properties support an efficient greedy selection algorithm and theoretical bounds on its utility. The conditions are essential to the claim: the paper establishes when the useful selection structure holds. Applications motivating the problem include feature selection, phase retrieval, and target localization.
icml-2019-submodular-observation-selecti.tldr: Van Trees-based criteria preserve quadratic measurement structure and, under specified conditions, enable greedy observation selection with utility guarantees.

paragraphs: Recurrent networks can perform similarly on a delayed classification task yet differ substantially when asked to remember information for longer delays. This paper investigates that discrepancy through hidden-state dynamics. The authors compare networks trained using different protocols, datasets, and architectures, allowing them to examine memory durability beyond ordinary task performance.

They associate each memory with a nearly stationary part of the dynamics called a slow point. The speed at these points predicts performance on longer delays across all tested datasets, protocols, and architectures. Tracking how slow points form also helps explain why different training protocols produce different abilities to preserve information over time.

The authors then use this relationship to design a regularization method that manipulates hidden-state speeds. They report a dramatic improvement in memory robustness over time. The contribution thus moves from describing where memories reside to identifying a measurable property that predicts their longevity and can be altered during training. The predictive evidence is established across the settings tested in the paper.
icml-2019-understanding-and-controlling-.tldr: Hidden-state slow-point speeds predict memory longevity in the tested recurrent networks and motivate regularization that substantially improves memory robustness.

paragraphs: Pretraining may appear unnecessary when a model trained from scratch achieves similar classification performance. This paper asks whether that comparison overlooks other benefits. It evaluates robustness and uncertainty estimation, examining aspects of model behavior that ordinary classification metrics may fail to capture even when their reported scores are similar.

The experiments cover corrupted labels, class imbalance, adversarial examples, detection of out-of-distribution inputs, and confidence calibration. Across this investigation, the authors demonstrate large gains from pretraining and find that those gains can complement methods designed specifically for the task. This makes pretraining relevant to both resistance to difficult conditions and the quality of a model’s uncertainty estimates.

The paper reports approximately a ten-percentage-point absolute improvement over the previous state of the art in adversarial robustness. In some cases, pretraining alone also surpasses prior state-of-the-art methods. These findings support including pretraining when evaluating robustness and uncertainty techniques, since differences in pretraining can materially affect the comparison even when conventional classification performance changes little.
icml-2019-using-pre-training-can-improve.tldr: Experiments show that pretraining can substantially improve robustness and uncertainty estimates even when standard classification metrics reveal little benefit.
